data.title: How a Bicycle Moves
data.subtitle: Discovering how your legs turn into wheels
data.overview: Have you ever wondered how pushing down with your feet makes a bicycle roll forward down the street? It is an amazing chain reaction of simple machines working together!

steps.title: Stepping on the Levers
steps.description: Your foot applies heavy weight and force onto the metal bar attached to the bicycle frame. This downward drop acts as a simple lever that forces the center axis to begin turning in a circle.
steps.imagePrompt: Close-up of a child sneaker pressing down on a silver metal bicycle pedal on a sunny sidewalk, natural afternoon lighting, realistic textures of rubber shoe tread and pitted metal.
steps.whatsHappening: The pedal acts as a lever arm, multiplying your leg strength into rotational force called torque.
steps.funFact: Your leg muscles can push with a force equal to three times your actual body weight when starting from a dead stop!
steps.purpose: It starts the rotational movement that the rest of the bicycle transfers directly to the rear wheel.

steps.title: Pulling the Metal Loop
steps.description: As your foot goes down, the metal arm rotates a large metal wheel covered in sharp metallic teeth. This toothed circle grabs onto a flexible loop of interlocking metal links.
steps.imagePrompt: Macro photograph of a shiny silver bicycle chain resting on the teeth of a large metal chainring, outdoors in daylight, showing oil sheen and metallic grain.
steps.whatsHappening: Teeth on the chainring hook into the gaps between individual metal links to pull the chain forward.
steps.funFact: A standard bicycle chain contains over 100 tiny moving parts that all bend together simultaneously.
steps.purpose: This connection carries the spinning energy from the front of the bike all the way to the back.

steps.title: Spinning the Rear Gear
steps.description: The interlocking metal links race backward and catch onto a much smaller set of teeth attached to the center of the back wheel. Because the back wheel gear is smaller, it whips around much faster than your feet are moving.
steps.imagePrompt: Close-up of a multi-speed bicycle cassette gear cluster on the rear wheel, photographed outdoors with natural light reflecting off the steel cogs.
steps.funFact: You can change gears to make pedaling feel like climbing a steep mountain or zooming down a flat highway!
steps.purpose: It multiplies your speed so the back wheel spins much faster than your feet.

steps.title: Rolling Across the Ground
steps.description: The fast-spinning center hub forces the outer rubber tire to rotate rapidly against the pavement. The friction between the rubber tread and the road pushes the entire bicycle forward into motion.
steps.imagePrompt: Low angle photograph of a bicycle tire rolling along a grey asphalt road, captured in bright daylight with dust particles visible in the air.
steps.funFact: A bicycle is one of the most efficient machines ever invented, turning over 90 percent of human leg energy into motion!
steps.purpose: This final action converts all the stored mechanical energy into forward travel.

summary.text: By linking your leg muscles to levers, chains, and gears, a bicycle transforms a simple downward push into fast, rolling transportation.
summary.keyTakeaway: Gears and chains work together to let small forces travel great distances and create high speeds.

quickFacts.duration: Less than one second per pedal stroke
quickFacts.whereItHappens: Along the drivetrain of the bicycle
quickFacts.funComparison: Over 90 percent efficient, beating almost every car engine!
quickFacts.energySource: Energy from food converted by your muscles
